Two brothers, named Thomas and John Quinn, were charged at Warrington Borough Court, on Saturday, with hating committed a breach of the peace by lighting with each other on the '27th July. One of the defendants said that he and his brother were discussing wit h some other uncertain points in connection: with the Purnell Commission. Because they (the two guinea) were Purnellites the other men wanted to settle the dispute by lighting with them. Thomas was quite willing to resort to fisticuffs. hut John was not, and in melee; touring to dissuade his brother the two got into a ! tight with each other. They were both stand over to keep the peace.

Some alarm Was occasional in Portsmouth on Tuesday upon the sailing of the fleet, when the Invincible and Black Prince were seen to crane into collision. There was a fresh brmve blowing at the time. The Black Prince received some damage on the port side, and the Invin- cible had all her headgear carried away. The Black Prince also lost her iniveratopmast and port booms. and her cutter 'Wan 6111a51104 to pieces. The Victory Fott some time past items of news on have continued to arrive from

Me. Egypt to the effect that Dervishes were marching northward and threatening an in- vasion of the country. General Gassratt was understood to be preparing to give them a warm reception when they came within striking dis- tance : but it WIIS scarcely thought that the encounter would result in such a decisive battle as that which took place m Saturday last The enemy fought bravely and desperately for seven hors; but they were ont-inamcuvred, and they were, besides, no match for well-armed and well- trained seldiers. It was a case with the bulk of theta of “do or die." We are told that NJ till, the Dervish leader, fought while there was any life in him, and finally fell pierced by a rifle bullet. Ah,ilul Ha LEM and all the principal Emirs died at their posts like mem" Weed, the latest in:counts state that every Dervish Emir, with the exceptionof I 4113, mu killed. Altogether sonic 1,500 perished on the side of the enemy, against as Anglo-Egyptian lossof 22 killed slid 131 wounded. It is not pleasant to think of this wholesale slaughter of Dervishes, with the knowledge that it adds to the thousands of lives which have been lost since nor occupatio al of Egypt; but if there is no other way than fighting it is better that a cam- paign should be shed, sherP, sod decisive— such ss the present campaign Ims proved. It must be borne in mind that the enemy were in this case the aggress,. ; and that there Wits no treatieg with them, since they marched on with a confidence dam of ignorance and fanaticism. It may be found that this will be the hot great struggle with the Suudanese. Egypt propen is making pnegress under the British Protectorate ; and if trade could be pened out up to Khartoum as lif old all would be well. The latest victory on the Nile will cer- tainly improve matters.

THE Poet LAUREATE colebrded his eightieth birthday, on Tuesday, Birthday. and who is there who does not wish him " Many happy returns?" It can be said of him, as he said of his predecessor, WORDSWORTH, that he titters nothing base. On the contrary, his comeptions of life, and love, and duty, are ennobling, and " inake for righteousness." He has lived it long life in an age winch is supposed to he the reverse of poetical, and yet he has been true as a 1,..et to Ow spirit of the age. Lord TENNYSON is essentially modern, yet how related he is felt to be to all the great OM'S Of the earth who are not for an sge, but for all time! Those who most • carefully study Ins verse lire struck with the fact that he is invariably td,reast, in his allusions, of the latest knowledge in science, whilst his familiarity with trees sod flowers is so great as to reveal that he is a loving and csreful student of botany. Careful he illways is there is evidence of cure even in his nowt brilliant work ; and in this respect he is in contrast with the " line carelessness " of
Shakespeare. The Laureate has described pm- veil. as

Jewels tire-words long That on the stretched fan-huger of all time Sparkle for ever and it in his merit that he hm added largely to ' the world's enaket of jewels. It will interest stedmits of Tennyson to learn that the fnintis- piece of " Scrilmer's Magazine," for A.ngnmt, is a striking portrait 44 the poet from a photog,rraph taken loot year. TiS verdict of "Guilty " which The Maybrick T 6, pronounced upon Mrs. MAvino.

_L.-- - at the Liverpool AA:sixes, on Wed- nesday, seems to have mine upon many p• • •, as a surprise. Them was an expectatio, , amongst those who had arrived at the oil., that Mrs. MAVERICK had poisoned her in order to get rid of him, that the case break down through disagreement amongst jury. There can he no vacation that the unhappy woman who is now under sentenm of death he, had a fair trial. Everything that could be said her favour was said by the most eminent edema, of the day and it is due even to the counsel the prosecution to say that he did not at my point press the evident') unduly against the , accused. Mr. Justice STKCIFLN, in slimming up. I whilst showing how damning in the main was the ! evidence against Mrs. MAVERICK, was studiously careful not to omit any point that might be regarded as in her favour. The jury had devoted themselves for seven days to the considemtion of the case in I all its- bearings : and that they should, within [ forty minutes of their retiring from the court. rotors, with a verdict of "Guilty;' shows that all , reasonable doubts in the case had been excluded from their minds. There is a dispositiou amongst si certain portion of the community to gees- hien the justice of the verdit_t ; and we notice with regret that the carriage of the fridge was I mobbed when his lordship left the court. But rowdy partisanship cannot munt_for much against • the judgment of twelve 'nen who for so many hours ' during so many days devoted themselves to the task of getting at the truth. That, they arrived at the truth, and that their verdict is a just no, we do Inot ourselves doubt. The- motive for the crime I was revealed in what the judge dulled "that terrible 1 letter" to her paramour,. the letter in which the adultress told the companion of her guilt that ; her husband was "sick into death.' That, as a matter of fact.he was not at. that looniest "sin , unto death " reveals ;is with a lightuing tlash what was within the darkness of-ber mind while the fact that he subsequently died from iirsenical poisoning suggests how. deliberately :mil how cruelly she carried out hercruel purpose. Arsenic in various bottles and preparations was found in her room, and it could not be explained away. It was•found when it should not have been formd in the medicine of the sick man; it was found in • the jug which had contained his sonp it was found in glycerine it wus found in ineat.juice it was on herapron,her handkerchiefmnd dressing-gown— and the trail of the serpent was over it all. The jury have declared Mrs. Maybriek guilty of the foul crime of murdering her husband by adminis- tering minion, and it is a verdict whiA is ' in amordance with the evidence.

A young man named William (molly tried the other evening to swallow a poker. There wan an inquest lin lies body on Tuesday. It not unfriopiently happens that a straight-backed per- son is referredto an "looking as if /IA swallowed piker" ; hut the actual pe'rfortimnee is rare; and, judging from Connolly's ease, the pestime is not likely to become popular.

General Boulanger is still alive, and, in a small way, kicking. He has issued a manifesto in which he -traverses the acmes:dims himight against him in the evidence to he submitted to this High , Court, and avers that all the charges east at him I are infamous slanders. This is something, hut it is not enough. If be would clear himself, he must go before the High Court. and meet evidence with evidence.

All is not lost to Liberalism even in Birmingham. At a meeting of the Town Council, on Tuesday, Councillor Clayton, Chalstonian Liberal, was nom- inated for the Mayoralty of the borough by 24 votes to 12 given for Councillor Follows, Conser- vative. It seems the Liberal Unionists on this OCIASIOII voted with the Liberals, and the Tories are wrathful. They hoped to make use of their Unionist allies in snatching this particular thes- nut from the tire.

From a paper read at the Bangor Diocesan ' Conference, it appears that, in Wales, Dissent is a long way ahead of the Church in literature as well as in noinhers. The Dissenters have thirteen weekly papers while the Church h:m mie only; and in monthly magazines the proportion ii that of ten to two. t!hurchnten are desirous of tanking con- verts in the Principality; hut perhaps they are right in concluding that it is not to be Roman- plishffl by providing material for the thinking faculties.

Despite the memorial to Lord Salisbury signed : by 40 Conservative members of Parliament. pray- ing for the withdrawal of the Tithes Bill the ! Governmenthave decided to prolong the session in , order to carry it. The Tories feel that it is hard on them that they should defer their holidays and disgust many of their constitutentsfor a miserable I measure which is pleasing only to the clergy. Radicals ender such circumstances would revolt but the Tories are slaves who, even while protest- ing, will respond to the whip of the master. Bank-Holiday was just so-so, or hardly an. lus this part of the country, Monday was a wet and altogether Ilinagreeable day but those who got away to Blacks.) and Southport seem to have found fine weather. The workpeople of the Penketh Tanning Co. put in full time. It was close on midnight when they reached Warrington the two buses awaiting them could not take all the party and there was a walk, for the remnant, of three miles. It was something, however, to beat the cooed, tel exclaim, whilst homeward bound—" What a day and night we are having !"

A settlement has been effected on the Kenmore estate through the medium of Rev. Canon Walsh, , parish priest of Rathmore The terms are—a re- ! duction of 25 per cent, where the tents exceed the : : poor law valuat on, evicted tenan.a to be reinstated, and all arrears wiped out on payment of one year's rent leas 25 per cent. In Killarney the Land 13oari1 Sub-Commissioners have given judgment in numerous eases, awanling reductions averag- Ml per cent. Results such as these are a revelation as to the way in which tenants have been robbed in the past ; and they explain, too, how it happens that they resist evictions which would rob them of their tenant right interest.

What with the opening of the Dee Bridge, and • the golden edding celebration at Hawarden, , Mr and Mrs. Gladstone had a busy time of it on ! Saturday. Mr. Gladstone's speech shows how I much he felt the congratulations and good wishes and how beautifully it finishes :—"God bless you ladies and gentlemen, friends and neighbours, in every relation of life, and if we have been united in the past, may we, through His grace and goodness, i be yet more united in the brief future that alone' can remain to us on earth, and in that longer future, through which, as I hope, the inhabitants of flawarden will be known as a virtuous and Christian, and advancing, and happy, and 'tud commmity of men."

MR. JEANS AND HIS COWS.—A LIVELY REPLY. Sir,—Plesseallow meafew lines in reply to the remarks modest the last meeting oldie Rural Sanitaly, Authority, and reported in your paper of last Saturday, in reference to my cow-keeping, of which I may say lam not at all ashamed. In the first place I thank you for doing what, as a lawyer, I cannot do myself, i.e., advertise myself and my profession. I have no doubt Mr. Wyndham Smith, as well as myself, will feel pleated at being thus made a little mare widely known as lawyers, and conse- quently open to business, than we otherwi should have been, on) that the good people of Lancashire and Che- shire will shortly be rushing to our respective offices. In the second place, I notice the playful references to the case in three Warrington papers and their bills of contents. The " Guardian" has it "Mr. Jeans and his cows—an interesting case." The "Observer" hat it "A solicitor's recreation—Should he be registered son milk- d.ler," and the "Examinee" has it "A Warrington lawyer objects to be registered as a milkseller." These were no doubt studiously worded to promote the sale of your papers, and I make no complaint about them, yet they remind me of a pantomime song lonee heard, the chorus of which was "It is funny, funny, very very funny." And now I will proceed to business. I do not object to being registered as a milkseller, in which there is nothing dishonourable (swept ,onletione.) but I submit that I as, not within the scope and intention of the orders and regulations under which milksellers are required to be registered, and if) am not, I do not mean to be coerced into registration, and thereby being made amenable to Mr. Inspector's poking his nose into y business. The question is one of law, and I am not influenced by nonsensical talk reported in the news- papers—as all the talk in the world, whether by parsons, or magistrates, or Jacks-hi-Offices, or men clothed with a little temporary authority, will not render me liable, if am not liable by law, and what they think, or who I am, does not make a pin difference. The regulations have for their object the registration of cowkeepers, dairymen, and purveyors of milk. The question is, am I one or the other within the meaning, scope, and inten- tion of those regulations? The mere fact of keeping cows, or the number of cows kept, has nothing whatever to do with the question. The Quern, or Prince of Wales, I submit, is not a cowkteper because she or he keeps cows. The business of a "cowkeepar " is well-known to be that of a man who keeps cows, generally not on land, but often in sheds in towns, and supplies milk to his customers u.s a milk-dealer and retailer of milk. A dairyman (better known as such in the South of Eng- ! land) is a man who rents and works other people's cows, and sells milk in like ina-dier, cow-keeper. A purve}orio one who pverh,..., goods and provides for the supply thereof to other people, and the thing pur- cha.sed " porveved." I suppose I may take it for granted that none of the gentlemen wbo talked no glibly about my being a purveyor, ever heard elan ancient officer of the Crown called the King's Purveyor, whose office it was to purchase or purvey provisions for the use of the lio.Auld. It would be a good thing if some people would caress good pocket dictionary, and preciously look at the meaning of the words they intend to use, so as not to diametrically misapply them u.. 4 did my friend Mr. Heaton, who contended that if I only sold six quarts of milks don) should be the purveyor, instead of my customer, Mr. Wilkinson, who purveys the same. The fact that I am not a dairyman or a purveyor will, I think, be conceded after fleabag,. . . .

It only remains therefore to see if I am a eowkeeper— and remember that the question to not tt do I keep eows " or " how many cows dot keep," but am I a cow- keeper such no is meant and intended by the regulations. I submit that I at, not. My business is not that of a markets:vv. I happen to own a few aeres of land I nay it with all humility and not boastfully). To pasture that land I limp a 'few COWA. The cows produce milk. Mr. Wilkinson, as a purveyor of milk, takm that milk, and takes it practically direct from the cows an it is put : into tin pail from the milk cans without being .brought inte the house. The questimn is does that constitute me a cowkeeper within the meaning of the regulations. If It does, I shall of course lace to submit to the regula- tions, or give up inilkselling. It is entirelya legal ques- tion, and I fear it is beyond the graspif anybody who spoke upon it, and would have to be derided by a calm, . . .

unbiassed judicial nand. I should certainly au a lawyer , not think of resisting " MCI authority," except In for as I COnsider myself not amenable to that authority. And, finally. referring to Mr. Jolley's remarks. I would ‘isly eav in the wonls id to very old writer, slightly altered and abbreviated for the oceasmn, 'Why. doth the heatlam rage "—and ...Lord, how hen he ptercased."—l am, yours tnily,

BY THE REV. B. NIOIMMSII VIL
7.-RISLEY PRESBYTERIAN CHAPEL.

Five miles from Warrington in a noth-easterly direction is the little village of Risley. 'the neiirest station to it is Padgate, from which it is about two and a half miles walk along • level road and through delightful scenery. The village gave its 11.411., to. or derived it from, a fanatic long resident here. It appears,' says canon Reines in Siiiities Cestp-, from the Culeheth Pedigree, accorately deduced and substantiated by deeds, that in the early part of the reign of Edward I. Robert, fourth son of Hugh de Ilindley, who hal obtained lands from Robert Banastre, married one of the four, daughters and, co-heiresses of (iihert de Culcheth, awl having obtained Risley with his wife, 88+1.1111ed that surname. The edate continued in that family until the last eentury, when it -was sold by John Riseley, gent, and is now held by John Ireland Blackbourne Rsg.'"To this env be added a sent- ence from Baines. Risley (Nil,- says he, the residence of a family of that name existing in the sixteenth century, has now disappearksh The lord- ship of Risley, after having been the property of grandfather, father, and sou, each named John . Risley, passed into the family of the Blackburnes, , and is now held by Richard.l/ewliorst,Esq., of Ken-' yen House." In the diaryof Roger Lowe, of Ashton- ' in-Make...field, from 141413 to 16741 there is a curious ' entry relating to one of • the Risleys. Under date March link, 166 d, Friday, the diarist says I went to the tunerall of !Bain Potter, daughter of Thos. Potter, and was interred at. Winwick. As we! earns into Winwick Church yard, Captain° Rieley's soldiers waretraininge,and when we ware att prayrs in t he church -upon the funerals occasion the souldiers discharged their musquets three times." The diarist was a.stauncli Presbyterian whose sense of propriety seems to have been shocked by the pre- sence and conduct of Captain Risley's soldiers in the grave yard during the funeral service. To this family we are indebted for the origin of Noncon- formity in this locality. The ___.... .

THOMAK RISLRY. M.A. was born August 27t h 1630. lie Was the son of Thomas Risley, gentleman, and Thomasin, his wife, dais liter of Henry [Althorn, of Winston. In the Parish ehttrchyani of Warrington may still he seen the tombstone of this couple upon which is the fol- lowing inscription :—" Here lyeth the body of T 11003149 Risley who was buried the 14th day of October, aged 82, 1670, and of Thomasin hie wife , who was buried the 26th day of July. aged 83, want- in, 3 Net-eke, 1681." How this branch of the family was connemed with the Risleys of Risley halt I do not know. The eldest son of Thomas and Thomasin Risley was.lchn Risley who a-as born in 1628. Ile was edueaterl at Pembroke College, Oxford, was afterwards fellow of New College, and died Janua.y 14, 1661. His brother the Rev. Thomas Risley, already named. was baptized at Newchurch as l "Thomas Mimi Thomas Risley Newto Rapti, lltth Septemh, 1630." His early edocution Was I received at the Warrington Grammar School unaer I Mr. Nathan Ashworth, whence he proceeded in 1040 to Pembroke College, where after four years he was I elected Fellow. He is said to have been much of a eausethere. aiming rataer to acquire nolid learning than fame." The Risley family were Episcopalians, but his leaning towards Nonconformity seems to have been early suspected. Upon the restoration of Charles 11. to the Throne royal visitors went down to the University to inqiiire into matters but Risley was confirmed in his Fellowship and the following instrument was drawn in his favour: We, having : received sufficient testimony of the honest life and conversation of Thomas Risley M.. 4, as also of his diligence in his studies, his progress and sufficiency in learning, and conformity to the doctrine and dis- cipline of the Church of England, t he government of this University, and the statutes of the college wherein he lives, do, by these presents, ratify, allow, and confirm the said Mr. Tim. Risley in his Fellowship, with all rights, dues, and all per- quisites thereunto belonging. inotaitlistanging any nullities, irregularities, or imperfections, which in a strict interpretation of the said college statutes, may be olojected Peri. lIOOD, ViCe-Can., NICHOLAS WoODWARD. S. Th. IL,THOMAS BARLOW D.D. Dated June 20,1001." I copy from Calamy a further account of this good man. He says '"Hit held his fellowship till Aug. 24, 1062, when he waa obliged to surrender, because lie could not comply with the act for uniformity. However their respect for him, and their unwillingness to . lose so valuable a member, prompted them to allow him a year to consider the case: in which inter val he examined the terms of conformity with great diligence and impartiality, that he might be able to satisfy others unwell as hie own conscience, that lie was not carried away by the prejudices of educa- tion. Upon Nov. 10, 1662, he was ordained deacon and presbyter the same day, by the Bishop of Nor- wich, who, in his certificate, gave him a very honourable character. But upon mature delibera- tion, he could not, for any place. be satisfied to came up to the conditions pre.scribtsl by the act. Ile retired therefore to his estate in the country. where, during the storm of persecution, he employed himself in preaching privately to ouch as scrupled conformity, and in visiting the sick, for whose sake he applied himself to the study of physic; by the practice of which, he the more effectually engaged their attention when be administered to their mil:, . . .

tual advice. After about four years, the Vice- chancellor of Oxford sent him a pressing invitation to return thither. promising him preferment to I encourage his conformity ; he had also good offers I made him by Dr. Hall and Dr. Sherlock of Win- wick ; but a regard to conscience hindered his acceptance. lie made a tolerable shift in the latter I end of the reign of Charles, and that of James. When liberty of conscience was granted, after the Revolution, his neighbours who had been his private auditors before, resolved themselves into a regulas society, and committed theinsel yea to his pastoral conduct, and he was vety useful among them by his ministerial performances and exemplary life and conversation."

Tradition has it that Mr. Risley held a coventicle frequently in a field close by the present chapel. Beyond this it is not known where the people wor- shipped until the erection of the chapel in 1707. In Matthew Henry's Diary there are notices of two ordination services, at which Mr. Rialey and other Lancashire notables were the ordainers. There was one such meeting at Knittsfonl on the 27th of September, 1692 ; and the 16th of June, 1702 "no la day of fasting and prayer, and impo.sition of hands in a very great congregation at Warring- ton," and "Mr. Risley concluded with a serious exhortation." In April, 1714, the Rev. William Ilanling, of Partington, 'was examined, approved, and allowed to preach as a candidate by Mr. Risley and Mr. Owen, of Warrington,with whom he lived." Mr. Risley died in 1716, an the eighty-sixth year of his age, and was buried in Risley chapel. yard. His tombstone is still in existence, but the inscription has been obliterated. The pre- sent minister, Rev. Wait. Dunn, however, who takes great interest in preserving any relics of the early history of the chapel, has placed upon it the following limo interred the body of the Revd. Thomas Risley, MA., Oxford. He 'eft the Church of England in 1662, and built Risky Chapel in 1707, I where he officiated up to his death. He died in I 1716, aged 86 years. 'The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance.' Psalm exii. 6." His funeral sermon was preached by his friend Dr. C. Owen, of Warrington, from the text 2 Kings ii. 12. This was dedicated to Mr. John Finley, and after- wards printed together with brief " Memoirs of kin life.' Mr. Risky did not contribute much to litera- ture, the only work from his pen known to exist is " The Cursed Family a treatise on the evil of neg- lecting family prayer." The celebrated John Howe wrote • preface to it, in which he gave some account of the author. Mt. Risley left at least two sons, Thomas and John. JOH N RINLNY

was horn January 29th, 1690, educated at filaagow, : and succeeded his father in the ministry at Risley , Chapel. Ile died September 3rd, 1743, and wris . buried like his father at Rieley Chapel. From his tombstone 1 copy the following Here littered the Body of the Revd. John Risley A.M., born Jan. 29th, 1690, aged 53, dy'd 34 of 5epr.,1742. Hannah the wife of John Risley, May 27th, 1730. Iler age 35. Ilannah the datighter of John and Hannah Risley, Nov. 12th, 1723." The REV. JOHN HARDY follows. Ile was trained by Dr. Bother= at Kendal, was the son of the Rev. Thomas Hardy, of llorwich, near Bolton, settled first at Bisphant near Blackpool, whence he removed to Risley. Ile died in 1748, and was followed by the RSV. SAMUEL WATRRHOUSR.

Of him 1 know nothing beyond what appears on the brass plate, inserted in his tombstone. The follow- ing is the copy of the inscription : Here rest the remains of Sam. Waterhouse, V. 0.51., who officiated as minister of this Society 14 years, with what fidelity and success will be manifest when irons Christ shall appear in glory. Obt. sth July, 1762,

:ETATIS 54.- There was a Roy. Mr. IVaterhouse at Walmsley, near B ,Iton, for many years. He appears to have left here about the time that Mr. Samuni Waterhouse began his ministry at Risky. It to therefore very probable he was the same person. The next mini...

RSV. THOMAS THRELKELD. was a remarkable character. Ile wag the son of the Rev. Samuel Threlkeld for several years minister at Penrith, and afterwards at Halifax. Thomas Threlkeld was born April P 2, 1739, and went. first to to be trained by De Ashworth, at tho Daventry Academy, then to Warrington, in 1757. In 172 be became minister at Risks', with a small and plain, but most harmonious, affectionate, and agreeable Society of Protestant Disventers." Here he married Miss Martha Wright, a member of his congregation. In IS he removed to Rochdale, where he laboured until his death which rook place on April Gth,ltital. His funeral sermon was tweet:lied at Rochdale on. the 13th of April by, his intimate friend,Dr. Barm, of Manchester. He was noted for his wonderful memory, and many curious stories about him have been preserved. On any passage being recited from the Bible he could,with unfailing ! accuracy, give the chapter and verse where it could • be found. Dr. Enfield once challenged him to tell. the place of a text upon which he had been preaching. Mr. Threlkeld called for a Bible and foand the pass- age saying Quote fair, sir, and you shall have a fair answer. Rat I knew that you had confounded two verses which stand at a considerable distance 'sander. You have doised the ;it It and 10th verses as though they were one" Ile wits also a good linguist. Nine or ten languages it is certainly known that he mad, not merely without difficulty but with profound and critical skill." Amongst other things it is mid that he was shortsighted— so mach so that lie tilt! not dare to ride on horse- back, because in that elevated position he could not see the ground. This made him somewhat shy and retiring. The information respecting the ministers at Risley after Mr. Threlkeld is exceedingly meagre and imperfect. I regret my efforts to give a correct list with the dates of settlement and resignation have not been attended with greater success.

A Mr. Harkeison succeeded Mr. Throlkeld at Risley concerning whom I have no information, lie could not, however, have been here long as Mr. Thelkeld only. left in 1770 and in 1779 or 1780 the Rev. John Aspmall was minister here. He had previously laboured at Walmaley for nearly twenty years. He died at Risley. The next minister is the Rev. Thomas Smith, who was trained for the Wesleyan ministry and laboured for a short time at ! Dukinfield. In June, 1797, he went to Stand, near ! Manchester, where he remained until 1811 in which year he removed to Park Lane, near Wigan. He left the ministry in 182." but at what period he was at Risley I do not know. I imagine it was ! before his settlement at Stand. Ile was followed , by a Mr. Lloyd who must again be dismissed as one ot the unknown ones—arile.s it was the same per- son that ministered at Doh Lane, near Manch,' or, ! and afterwards became an eminent banker. Ilia successor was the Rey. G. W. Elliott, who left some- time before ISIA for Rochdale. Ile was of terwards minister at Prescot Unitarian limpid. The next minister was the R.,. W. Morris who was at Risley De2.l, and he was followed by the Rey. Joins Marriott. . .

• Important theological changes came over many of these old Presbyterian Congregational Churches during the seeond half of last century. Prom , Trinitarianism they went into Arianism awl thence into Unitarianism. And Risley did what many others did. Since the days of Thomas Threlkehl, if not before Arianism began to show itself, and, in the days of Mr. Marriott, Risley had become thoroughly Unitarian. In DM Mr. Joseph Doming and Mr. Jonathan Doming, of Colcheth, nssisted by : the Into Mr. Belmont, of Warrington, tiled a peti- tion in Chancery to remove Mr. Marriott from Risley and also the Unitarian Trustees. The petition was successful awl in 18:44 they were ejected. The following new misters were appointed .—llugh Ralph LL.D., John Park and Alexander Monro, Presbyterian ministers Thomas McGill, Duncan Dibh, Homy Gordon, Alexander Boggle, William Mellaffie, and Robert Barbour, merchants. . .

From this date Risley becomes a part of the PresbyterianChnrch of England and its ministers are Presbyterian. In 1838 the Rev. Alexander Rennison began duty here: be resigned in 1844. Ile was succeeded by the Rev. William Forster in the same year, whole spoken of non most scholarly man. Ile left in 183$, and now resides at Bowden without charge. In the some year Dr. Robinson followed and remained until 1866. Ile was succeeded by the

HMV. JOHN CI.NLAND in that year. Mr. Cleland had previously laboured at Bolton. and Douglas, Isle of Man. Ile resigned ' his charge at Risley in MI, and lived in retire- ment at Warrington until his death, which tools place in Feb. 1888, at the ripe age of 84 years. The , present minister, the REV. WILLIAM IWNN,

was ordained at North Sunderland, 'in Jan., 1865, and commenced duty at Risley in July, 1885. ! On being ejected from Risley the Unitarians ! erected a chapel at Croft ; a small village some two or three miles further north. Its history does not come within the scope of these papers. Risley Chapel, as already stated, was built in 1707. The trust deed bears Into March 25th, 1707, and is an indenture between' Thomas Risley, of Culchett, in the County of Lancaster, clerk°, Catherine his wife, and Thomas Risley, son and heir apparent of him, the said Thomas Risley, of the one part, and John Glove, Peter Doming, George Monks, William Bershall, Christopher Lythgoe, John Unsworth, and William Widows, all of them of Culchett and Kenyon, in the said County, yeomen, of the other par;," and states that the chapel was about to be erected upon a piece of land called Fifty Croft in Cross-lane, in Culchett bear the dwelling house of the said Themes Risley." It stands in a beautifully retired spot, is "away. from towns and cities" and if not exactly " within the wood "is yet well sheltered by trees. There is a large graveyard in front, which contains many memorials of the dead, some of which are of considerable age. The building is low, and in its long side there are two entrances which face the road. The bell tower is on the left gable, and,abutting the chapeLto the right,is a small vestry used for prayer meetings. One aisle cuts the chapel in two, on both sides of which lie the old pews, deep, and straight backed. Enteting by the vestry side, the pulpit is a little to the light. It differs from most of the old Presbyterian pulpits in an important respect. It is quite miniature, whereas Dr. 11 alley says that they were " high." "massive," and" broad,' and in most instances, if not all, had three decks. If this be the very one in which Mr. Risley preached, forsome reason or other he differed from moat of the so-called Presbyterian ministers of the time in his ideas of what the pulpit should be. On some of the pew doors appear the initials of the original occupants with the dates. The following are copied: -M. W. 1707; P. D. 1706 ; It. D. 1788 ; R. L. 1700; and on one pew appears the date 1758. I cannot account for the dates 1706 on the pew doors when the chapel was only erected in 1707 tulle. they point to an earlier place of worship in which they had been used. During Mr. Dunn's ministry the old n indows have been removed and the present large- paned ones inserted II which give to the chapel a light and comfortable appearance. Ile has also, put round the graveyard a good mm railing where formerly WWI nothing but an imperfect hedge fence. ' Rut mainly the chapel is as it was in the days of Mr. Risley, and is about as interesting and ancient looking as any I have seen. According to Sr.l Evan's list of Presbyterian Chapels Mr. Risley had a con- gregation of 250 persons and in it were sixteen county voters. Its sitting capacity to-day 1 imagine would to-pretty well tried with 200 people. There is a congregation of 30 in the morning and 60 or 70 in the afternoon. From the Rirley triage it receives as endowment ZII, and from the Patten trusts £B. It only remains for me to say that for some of the foregoing particulars I am indebted to a paper in' Local Gleanings " for 1876 contributed by J. I'. Rylands Eq.. F.S.A. -•
Nest article will be on Rainford Congregational Church.

A SHUNTING ACCIHNNT AT EARLESTOWN. A somewhat alarming accident occurred on one of the sidings near the Viaduct Waggon Works, liarlestown, At an early hour on Wednesday morn- ing. The engine of a goods train was engaged shunting some of the waggons, and the driver, intended to run on another set of rails, put on steam. From some cause, however, the engine dashed into the stop-buffers at the end of the sid- ing ;and with a loud crash completely demolished theft, levelling the block to the ground. The loco- motive left the rails and was embedded a couple of feet in the ground. It sustained some damage about the buffers, but happily the driver and stoker escaped unhurt. A break down gang was sent for to Warrington, and the engine was replaced on the siding about four hours later. There was no inter- ruption or delay in the ordinary traffic as the acci- I dent happened clear of the main lines.

In the a:Leery Division of the Iligh Com, o'f Justice, yesterday, before Mr. Justice Chitty, the Attorney-Gen- eral said he had a motion in the matter of the Manches- ter Ship Canal ; betas his learned friend, Sir 11. Davey, Q.C., had not seen his affidavit he could not Ming :in the motion in the sense of having it determined that day. The allegation on the affidavits was that the defendants were going on building the embankment con- i Gary to his lordship's recent order and without making 1 the tidal openings. It was arranged that, failing the I motion being disposed of by the vacation judge, it should he heard on the secota motion day after, the vacation. A SHIP CANAL FOR THE EAST COAST. •

The peopled Sheffield and South Yorkshire are to have their ship canal to theeast coast. A bill prosnotod by an influential committee of merchants and manufacturers fur the purchase of else Painting" navigations" and their enlargennunt into a canal capable of admitting veseels of considerable tonnage passed through the penultimate stage in Parliament on Tuesday. The Sheffield Railway Company, who are the owners of the " navis,sations," objected to Icing count:adsorby bought out, bust the Chairman of the Committee, in announcing that thuu was pAussusi, added that the Committee had come to that decision on grounds of public policy. The heavy trades of Sheffield and the district expect to derive immense benefit from the new canal.

.... ..... The first annual athletic festival in connection with the Manchester Ship Canal (No. 7 section) Cricket and , Lou., Tennis Club was held on Satacidalr, at hiam, in favourable weather. The entries were fairly numerous. Isome events lot ing competitors from various sections of the CII.IIAI. Nothwitlistanding the threatening state of I the weather about noon a large number of persons were present, and everything passed off successfully. While the various contffits were in progress the Carrington and Iclam brus bands played selections of music. Siete of the events were very keenly contested, especially was tins the case m the LOO yards (final) and TX yards flat races. The arrangements were carried out by •Committee con.sisting of Messrs. W. 0. E. Minute-King. W. Taylor, C. V. Fondle. E. R. Stokoe, C. R. Sayers, M. Talbot, C. F. Philips, and C. Holmes. The stewards were Sr. Jago, Messrs. C. E. Carden, E. R. Mid, H. R. Hillier, W. - -- On Monday the employes of Mr. Thomas Molyneux, grocer, Market-at.. Earlestown, with a number of friends, had a picnic to I late. Notwith- standing the showery weather tine ride was a picas- Intone, and the attractions of the ancient village were inspected. Tea WM served at the ehilde of lisle Hotel, after which the return journey was commenced. The waggonette was provided ny Mr. Walton, of Cross-lane. llooma Goon TEMPLARS AT NRWTON LAN..

About :3011 members and friends of the Bootle " Offspring of hope" lodge of flood Templars had a picnic to Newton Lake on Saturday. They arrived by train and were accompanied by the life and drum band in connection with the lodge. They appeared to spend a pleasant afiernoon notwithstanding the showers of rain which foil. During the inclement weather they were granted the use of St. Peter's school.

PRESCOT FLOWER Snow.—Ou Thursday week the fifth exhibition of the Present and District Horticultural Society was held in a field at Parkside, Proseot, kindly lent by Mr. W. Goldsworth, jun. The weather was fine and the show was a groat success. Between ETO and £BO were offered in prizes and the exhibits amounted to nearly TOO, being 200 of an increase on last year. A rapacious tent had been erected by Mr. Price Owen, and there was an inthosing display. The judges were Mr. John Jellico (Wmilton), Mr. Was. Tunnington (Allerton),Mr. A. H. Cox (Wavertree), and Mr. W. Durant (ganiner to Mrs. W. L. Evan.s). The band of Use 2nd V.8.0.L.11., under the conductorship of Band- master Hall, discoursed selections to the enjoyment of the visitors.

PIIMSCOT PETTY S.SIOKS.—At the Present Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Mr. W. L. McClure and Mr. A. K. Gladstone, Jane Hayes, a married woman, living at Springfield Cottages, Rixleston, was charged with unlawfully wounding Elimbeth Owen, a neighbour, on the preViolls Friday night. Mr. J. o... Swift prosecuted and Mr. Dyson defended. It was alleged that the prisoner struck the promTutrix a severe blow on the head with a stick ; and caused a deep cut on her fore- head with sane sharp instrument. It was stated that the prisoner mad a knife in her band. On b ing charged with the offence prisoner Saad 010 did it with a beck. The prisoner was committed for trial at tine sessions, and was ashnittml to bail.—ltarold Vivian Evansoif Rainhill, was fined 15s. and costs in each of two cases, for neglect- ing to take out the necessary carriage and man servant licenses—Bridget Gilligan and Kate Gilligan, her grand- daughter.were charged with stealing a pair of blunts frt. the shop dorr of Mr. J. S. Sanders. Bridget W. fined 55., and the charge against Kato was dismissed.— Ellen Siddall, a tramp, was charged with stealing a chemise, value 4d., the property of Mary AAR., from a lodging house in Iligh-st., Prem.. She was fined ss. Mary McAlyunn was charged with unlawfully wounding Francis Mannion, a collier, by striking noun the head with St stone and causing a serious wound.
